entry.title: The Next Decade of AI: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities

link.title: The Next Decade of AI: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities

entry.content:
A decade of deep learning has transformed what’s possible. LLMs write code, diffusion models create art, and AI systems increasingly assist in scientific discovery. What comes next? This post explores emerging trends, fundamental challenges, and opportunities for the next era of AI.

Where We Are

The Current Landscape

Foundation models: Pre-trained on massive data, adapted to tasks via prompting or fine-tuning. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama represent this paradigm.

Multimodal AI: Vision, language, audio in unified models. GPT-4V, Gemini can understand images and text together.

AI for science: AlphaFold solved protein folding. AI accelerates drug discovery, materials science, climate modeling.

Agentic systems: LLMs with tools, memory, and autonomy. Early examples of AI that can act, not just respond.

Emerging Trends

1. Inference-Time Compute

Current scaling focuses on training compute. Emerging research scales inference:

  • Test-time training: Adapt at inference
  • Chain-of-thought: More reasoning steps = better results
  • Monte Carlo Tree Search for reasoning

The shift: from “bigger model” to “more thinking.”

2. Multimodal Everything

Models that natively understand all modalities:

  • Text, images, audio, video together
  • Physical understanding (robotics)
  • Actions (code execution, tool use)

3. Efficient AI

Making AI accessible:

  • Smaller models with distillation
  • Quantization (4-bit, even 1-bit)
  • Edge deployment (on-device inference)
  • Cheaper training (data efficiency, architecture improvements)

4. Personalized AI

AI tuned to individuals:

  • On-device learning from user behavior
  • Preference learning from feedback
  • Privacy-preserving personalization

5. AI Agents in Production

Moving from demos to real systems:

  • Reliable tool use
  • Memory and context management
  • Multi-agent collaboration
  • Safety and oversight

6. World Models

Learning physics and causality:

  • Video prediction as world modeling
  • Planning through simulation
  • Transfer from virtual to real

Fundamental Challenges

Reasoning and Planning

LLMs pattern-match more than reason:

  • Struggle with novel problems
  • Inconsistent on multi-step logic
  • Limited causal understanding

Potential solutions: Neuro-symbolic integration, explicit planning modules, test-time compute.

Reliability and Hallucination

Models confidently generate false information:

  • Can’t reliably know what they don’t know
  • Hallucination rate varies unpredictably

Potential solutions: Retrieval-augmented generation, uncertainty quantification, grounding in knowledge bases.

Alignment and Safety

As AI becomes more capable:

  • Ensuring AI does what we intend
  • Preventing misuse
  • Maintaining human oversight

Potential solutions: Constitutional AI, RLHF improvements, interpretability research.

Data Limitations

Models trained on internet data:

  • Biases and misinformation
  • Static knowledge (cutoff dates)
  • Limited coverage of specialized domains

Potential solutions: Synthetic data, continual learning, curated datasets.

Opportunities

AI for Scientific Discovery

  • Hypothesis generation
  • Experiment design
  • Literature synthesis
  • Accelerating R&D cycles

AI-Augmented Work

  • Coding assistants that understand entire codebases
  • Writing tools that maintain voice and style
  • Research assistants that synthesize literature
  • Domain-specific copilots

Democratizing Expertise

  • Medical advice in underserved areas
  • Legal guidance for those who can’t afford lawyers
  • Education personalized to each learner
  • Translation and accessibility

New Interfaces

Beyond chat:

  • Voice-first experiences
  • Visual understanding (AR/VR)
  • Ambient intelligence
  • AI-native applications

What ML Practitioners Should Learn

Technical Skills

  • LLM fine-tuning and prompting: Core capability
  • Efficient inference: Quantization, distillation, serving
  • Evaluation: Measuring what matters for your application
  • Retrieval systems: RAG and beyond
  • Safety and alignment: Guardrails, red-teaming

Meta-Skills

  • Keeping up: The field moves fast
  • Experimentation: Try new approaches quickly
  • Systems thinking: ML in context of full stack
  • Uncertainty: Knowing what you don’t know

Looking Forward

Near-Term (1-3 years)

  • Agents become practical for real tasks
  • Multimodal as default
  • Efficiency improvements democratize access
  • AI regulation takes shape

Medium-Term (3-7 years)

  • More reliable reasoning
  • Continuous learning from deployment
  • Specialized domain AI
  • Human-AI collaboration norms established

Long-Term (7+ years)

Questions more than predictions:

  • How general will AI become?
  • What economic impacts emerge?
  • How does education adapt?
  • What new risks surface?

Summary

AI is at an inflection point—capable enough to be useful, not yet reliable enough for full autonomy. Key takeaways:

  • Inference-time compute and multimodality are emerging directions
  • Reliability, reasoning, and alignment remain open challenges
  • Massive opportunities in science, work augmentation, and access

The future is being built by practitioners who understand both capabilities and limitations. Stay curious, stay humble, and keep building.

Further Reading:

  • AI research labs’ annual reports (OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic)
  • State of AI Report (annual)
  • AI Alignment Forum
  • Your own experiments—nothing teaches like building

entry.title: ML Platform Engineering: Building the Infrastructure for ML at Scale

link.title: ML Platform Engineering: Building the Infrastructure for ML at Scale

entry.content:
Behind every successful ML system is platform infrastructure: feature stores, training pipelines, model registries, and serving systems. ML platform engineering enables data scientists to ship models faster while maintaining reliability and governance.

Introduction and Motivation

Individual ML models are now routine. The challenge is operating hundreds of models reliably: keeping features fresh, retraining on schedule, serving with low latency, and monitoring for drift.

ML platforms abstract these operational concerns, letting data scientists focus on modeling while the platform handles everything else.

Core Components

Feature Store

Centralized feature management:

Feature engineering: Compute features from raw data. Feature serving: Low-latency access at inference time. Point-in-time correctness: Historical feature values for training. Reuse: Share features across models and teams.

┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│   Offline   │───▶│    Feature   │◀──▶│   Online    │
│   Store     │    │    Store     │    │   Store     │
│   (Data     │    │              │    │   (Redis)   │
│   Lake)     │    │              │    │             │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └─────────────┘
       │                  │                   │
       ▼                  ▼                   ▼
┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│  Training   │    │    Feature   │    │   Model     │
│  Pipelines  │    │   Discovery  │    │   Serving   │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └─────────────┘

Training Infrastructure

Experiment tracking: Log parameters, metrics, artifacts. Distributed training: Multi-GPU, multi-node. Hyperparameter optimization: Automated search. Pipeline orchestration: DAGs of training steps.

Model Registry

Version control: Track model versions and lineage. Metadata: Training data, parameters, metrics. Promotion: Stage models through environments. Governance: Approval workflows, audit logs.

Serving Infrastructure

Inference: Real-time (online) and batch (offline). Scaling: Auto-scale based on traffic. A/B testing: Route traffic to model versions. Monitoring: Latency, errors, model performance.

Practical Implementation

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List, Any
import hashlib
import json

# Feature Store abstraction
@dataclass
class Feature:
    name: str
    entity: str  # e.g., "user", "item"
    value_type: str  # "float", "int", "string"
    description: str

class FeatureStore:
    """Simplified feature store implementation"""

    def __init__(self, offline_store, online_store):
        self.offline_store = offline_store  # e.g., BigQuery, Snowflake
        self.online_store = online_store    # e.g., Redis, DynamoDB
        self.registry = {}

    def register_feature(self, feature: Feature, transformation: str):
        """Register a feature definition"""
        self.registry[feature.name] = {
            'feature': feature,
            'transformation': transformation,
            'version': 1
        }

    def materialize(self, feature_name: str, start_date: str, end_date: str):
        """Compute and store feature values"""
        feature_def = self.registry[feature_name]
        # Execute transformation, write to offline store
        # Then sync to online store for recent values
        pass

    def get_online_features(self, entity_ids: List[str],
                           feature_names: List[str]) -> Dict:
        """Get features for serving (low latency)"""
        # Lookup from online store
        return self.online_store.multi_get(entity_ids, feature_names)

    def get_historical_features(self, entity_df, feature_names: List[str],
                                 timestamp_col: str):
        """Point-in-time join for training"""
        # Join features at correct historical timestamps
        return self.offline_store.point_in_time_join(
            entity_df, feature_names, timestamp_col
        )


# Model Registry
class ModelRegistry:
    """Track model versions and metadata"""

    def __init__(self):
        self.models = {}

    def register_model(self, name: str, version: str,
                      artifacts: Dict, metadata: Dict):
        """Register a trained model"""
        key = f"{name}:{version}"
        self.models[key] = {
            'name': name,
            'version': version,
            'artifacts': artifacts,  # Paths to model files
            'metadata': metadata,    # Training params, metrics
            'stage': 'development',
            'created_at': '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'
        }
        return key

    def promote_model(self, name: str, version: str, target_stage: str):
        """Promote model to staging/production"""
        key = f"{name}:{version}"
        if key in self.models:
            self.models[key]['stage'] = target_stage
            # Could trigger deployment here

    def get_production_model(self, name: str):
        """Get the production version of a model"""
        for key, info in self.models.items():
            if info['name'] == name and info['stage'] == 'production':
                return info
        return None


# Training Pipeline
class TrainingPipeline:
    """Orchestrate training workflow"""

    def __init__(self, feature_store: FeatureStore,
                 model_registry: ModelRegistry):
        self.feature_store = feature_store
        self.model_registry = model_registry
        self.experiment_tracker = {}

    def create_training_dataset(self,
                                entity_df,
                                feature_names: List[str],
                                target: str):
        """Create training data with features"""
        # Get historical features
        features = self.feature_store.get_historical_features(
            entity_df, feature_names, 'timestamp'
        )
        return features

    def train(self, config: Dict):
        """Execute training run"""
        run_id = hashlib.md5(
            json.dumps(config, sort_keys=True).encode()
        ).hexdigest()[:8]

        # Track experiment
        self.experiment_tracker[run_id] = {
            'config': config,
            'metrics': {},
            'status': 'running'
        }

        # Training logic here...

        return run_id

    def log_metric(self, run_id: str, name: str, value: float):
        self.experiment_tracker[run_id]['metrics'][name] = value

    def register_model(self, run_id: str, model_name: str,
                       artifacts: Dict):
        """Register trained model"""
        experiment = self.experiment_tracker[run_id]
        version = f"run_{run_id}"

        self.model_registry.register_model(
            name=model_name,
            version=version,
            artifacts=artifacts,
            metadata={
                'config': experiment['config'],
                'metrics': experiment['metrics']
            }
        )

        return version


# Serving Infrastructure
class ModelServer:
    """Handle model serving"""

    def __init__(self, feature_store: FeatureStore):
        self.feature_store = feature_store
        self.loaded_models = {}

    def load_model(self, name: str, version: str, artifacts: Dict):
        """Load model for serving"""
        key = f"{name}:{version}"
        # Load model from artifacts
        self.loaded_models[key] = {
            'model': None,  # Actual model object
            'features': artifacts.get('features', []),
            'version': version
        }

    def predict(self, model_name: str, entity_ids: List[str]) -> List[float]:
        """Get predictions for entities"""
        # Find active model
        model_info = None
        for key, info in self.loaded_models.items():
            if key.startswith(model_name):
                model_info = info
                break

        if not model_info:
            raise ValueError(f"No loaded model for {model_name}")

        # Get features
        features = self.feature_store.get_online_features(
            entity_ids, model_info['features']
        )

        # Inference
        predictions = model_info['model'].predict(features)

        return predictions

Best Practices

Self-Service

Let data scientists work independently:

  • Templated pipelines
  • Feature discovery
  • One-click deployment

Observability

Monitor everything:

  • Feature freshness
  • Training metrics
  • Serving latency
  • Model performance over time

Governance

Control model lifecycle:

  • Approval workflows
  • Data lineage
  • Audit trails
  • Access controls

Reliability

Design for failure:

  • Automated rollback
  • Fallback models
  • Circuit breakers
  • Chaos testing

Summary

ML platforms enable reliable, scalable ML operations. Key takeaways:

  • Feature stores ensure consistency between training and serving
  • Model registries track versions and enable governance
  • Automation and self-service accelerate iteration

Further Reading:

  • Uber’s Michelangelo, Airbnb’s Bighead, Spotify’s ML platform papers
  • Feast feature store documentation
  • MLflow, Kubeflow documentation
entry.summary: Behind every successful ML system is platform infrastructure: feature stores, training pipelines, model registries, and serving systems. ML platform engineering enables data scientists to ship models faster while maintaining reliability and governance.

entry.title: Causal Discovery: Algorithms for Learning Causal Structure from Data

link.title: Causal Discovery: Algorithms for Learning Causal Structure from Data

entry.content:
Can we discover causal relationships from data alone? Causal discovery algorithms attempt to learn the causal graph structure—which variables cause which—from observational or experimental data. This is among the most ambitious goals in machine learning.

Introduction and Motivation

Most causal inference assumes a known causal graph. But where does the graph come from? Domain experts provide structure, but this doesn’t scale: we can’t manually specify relationships among thousands of variables.

Causal discovery attempts to learn the graph from data. While impossible in complete generality (correlation doesn’t imply causation), under certain assumptions, we can make progress.

The Goal

Learn a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) $G$ where:

  • Nodes are observed variables
  • Edges represent direct causal effects
  • $X \rightarrow Y$ means “X directly causes Y”

From this graph, we can:

  • Identify confounders
  • Determine adjustment sets
  • Answer causal queries

Key Assumptions

Causal Markov Condition

Every variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents: \(X \perp \text{NonDesc}(X) | \text{Parents}(X)\)

Faithfulness

All and only the independencies in the data are entailed by the graph. (No “accidental” cancellations.)

Causal Sufficiency

No unmeasured common causes. (Can be relaxed with some algorithms.)

Algorithm Families

Constraint-Based (PC, FCI)

Use conditional independence tests to learn skeleton, then orient edges.

PC Algorithm:

  1. Start fully connected
  2. Remove edge X—Y if independent given some subset
  3. Orient v-structures: X → Z ← Y when X—Z—Y and X,Y not adjacent
  4. Apply orientation rules

Score-Based (GES, CAM)

Search over DAG space, maximizing a score (BIC, BGe): \(\text{Score}(G) = \log P(D|G) - \text{complexity}(G)\)

GES (Greedy Equivalence Search):

  1. Forward phase: Add edges greedily
  2. Backward phase: Remove edges greedily

Functional Causal Models

Assume specific functional form (linear, ANM), exploit asymmetries.

LiNGAM (Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model): \(X = BX + \epsilon\)

Non-Gaussianity of errors enables causal direction identification.

Practical Implementation

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from itertools import combinations

class PCAlgorithm:
    """Simplified PC algorithm for causal discovery"""

    def __init__(self, alpha=0.05):
        self.alpha = alpha

    def conditional_independence_test(self, X, Y, Z, data):
        """Test X ⊥ Y | Z using partial correlation"""
        if len(Z) == 0:
            # Marginal correlation
            r, p = stats.pearsonr(data[X], data[Y])
            return p > self.alpha

        # Partial correlation via residuals
        X_resid = self._residualize(data[X], data[list(Z)])
        Y_resid = self._residualize(data[Y], data[list(Z)])
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(X_resid, Y_resid)
        return p > self.alpha

    def _residualize(self, y, X):
        """Get residuals of y ~ X"""
        from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
        model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
        return y - model.predict(X)

    def learn_skeleton(self, data, variables):
        """Learn undirected skeleton"""
        n = len(variables)
        adjacency = {v: set(variables) - {v} for v in variables}
        separating_sets = {}

        depth = 0
        while depth < n - 1:
            for (X, Y) in list(combinations(variables, 2)):
                if Y not in adjacency[X]:
                    continue

                # Test conditioning sets of size 'depth'
                neighbors = adjacency[X] - {Y}
                if len(neighbors) < depth:
                    continue

                for Z in combinations(neighbors, depth):
                    if self.conditional_independence_test(X, Y, set(Z), data):
                        # Remove edge
                        adjacency[X].discard(Y)
                        adjacency[Y].discard(X)
                        separating_sets[(X, Y)] = set(Z)
                        separating_sets[(Y, X)] = set(Z)
                        break

            depth += 1

        return adjacency, separating_sets

    def orient_edges(self, adjacency, separating_sets, variables):
        """Orient v-structures and apply rules"""
        directed = {v: {'parents': set(), 'children': set()}
                   for v in variables}
        undirected = {v: set(adjacency[v]) for v in variables}

        # Find v-structures: X → Z ← Y where X,Y not adjacent
        for Z in variables:
            neighbors = list(undirected[Z])
            for (X, Y) in combinations(neighbors, 2):
                if Y in adjacency[X]:  # X and Y adjacent
                    continue

                sep_set = separating_sets.get((X, Y), set())
                if Z not in sep_set:  # Z is collider
                    # Orient X → Z ← Y
                    directed[Z]['parents'].add(X)
                    directed[Z]['parents'].add(Y)
                    directed[X]['children'].add(Z)
                    directed[Y]['children'].add(Z)
                    undirected[Z].discard(X)
                    undirected[Z].discard(Y)
                    undirected[X].discard(Z)
                    undirected[Y].discard(Z)

        return directed, undirected

    def fit(self, data):
        """Full PC algorithm"""
        variables = list(data.columns)

        # Step 1: Learn skeleton
        adjacency, sep_sets = self.learn_skeleton(data, variables)

        # Step 2: Orient edges
        directed, undirected = self.orient_edges(adjacency, sep_sets, variables)

        return {
            'directed': directed,
            'undirected': undirected,
            'adjacency': adjacency
        }


def generate_linear_scm_data(n_samples=1000):
    """Generate data from known linear SCM"""
    np.random.seed(42)

    # True graph: X → Y → Z, X → Z
    X = np.random.randn(n_samples)
    Y = 0.8 * X + np.random.randn(n_samples) * 0.5
    Z = 0.5 * X + 0.6 * Y + np.random.randn(n_samples) * 0.5
    W = np.random.randn(n_samples)  # Independent

    import pandas as pd
    return pd.DataFrame({'X': X, 'Y': Y, 'Z': Z, 'W': W})


# Example
data = generate_linear_scm_data()
pc = PCAlgorithm(alpha=0.05)
result = pc.fit(data)

print("Learned structure:")
print("Directed edges:")
for v, info in result['directed'].items():
    for parent in info['parents']:
        print(f"  {parent} → {v}")

print("\nUndirected edges:")
for v, neighbors in result['undirected'].items():
    for n in neighbors:
        if v < n:  # Print each edge once
            print(f"  {v} — {n}")

Equivalence Classes

Many DAGs encode the same conditional independencies:

Markov Equivalence Class: DAGs with same skeleton and v-structures.

We can only learn up to the equivalence class from observational data. Interventional data can break ties.

Challenges

Finite Sample

Independence tests can fail with limited data. Use regularization, bootstrap.

Scaling

$O(n^k)$ for conditioning set size $k$. Modern variants use local search.

Latent Confounders

Violate causal sufficiency. FCI algorithm handles this but recovers less structure.

Nonlinear Relationships

Linear methods miss nonlinear dependencies. Kernel-based, neural approaches exist.

Summary

Causal discovery attempts to learn causal structure from data. Key takeaways:

  • Constraint-based methods use independence tests
  • Score-based methods search DAG space
  • Can only learn up to equivalence class from observational data

Further Reading:

  • Spirtes, Glymour & Scheines, Causation, Prediction, and Search
  • Peters, Janzing & Schölkopf, Elements of Causal Inference
  • Causal Discovery Toolbox (CDT) Python library
entry.summary: Can we discover causal relationships from data alone? Causal discovery algorithms attempt to learn the causal graph structure—which variables cause which—from observational or experimental data. This is among the most ambitious goals in machine learning.

entry.title: Agentic AI: Building Autonomous Systems That Reason and Act

link.title: Agentic AI: Building Autonomous Systems That Reason and Act

entry.content:
In 2023, an AI agent autonomously completed a software engineering task that would have taken a human hours—writing code, running tests, fixing bugs, and iterating until it worked. This wasn’t science fiction; it was AutoGPT, one of the first agentic AI systems to capture public imagination.

Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift: from single-turn Q&A to autonomous systems that plan, execute tools, and iterate toward goals. These agents combine LLM reasoning with code execution, web search, API calls, and feedback loops.

From coding assistants to research agents to customer service automation, agentic systems are the next wave of AI applications. This post covers how to build them.

Introduction and Motivation

LLMs are impressive at generating text, but real-world tasks require action: searching databases, executing code, calling APIs, and iterating based on results. Agentic AI bridges this gap by building systems that can autonomously pursue goals.

From coding assistants to research agents to customer service automation, agentic systems represent the next wave of AI applications.

Core Components

The Agent Loop

At a high level, an agent repeatedly observes the world, thinks about what to do next, and acts using tools:

Figure: Agentic AI loop showing how Observe, Think, and Act steps interact with tools and feed back into new observations.

  1. Observe: Receive task or feedback from environment
  2. Think: Reason about what to do next
  3. Act: Execute tool or produce output
  4. Iterate: Process results, continue or terminate

Tool Use

Agents extend LLM capabilities with tools:

  • Code execution: Run Python, SQL, bash
  • Search: Web search, document retrieval
  • APIs: External services, databases
  • File operations: Read, write, modify

Memory

Agents need context beyond single interactions:

  • Short-term: Conversation history, recent actions
  • Long-term: Persistent knowledge, learned patterns
  • External: Retrieved documents, databases

Planning

Breaking down complex tasks:

  • Task decomposition: Split goal into subtasks
  • Dependency management: Order subtasks correctly
  • Backtracking: Recover from failed paths

Agent Architectures

ReAct (Reason + Act)

Interleave reasoning and actions:

Thought: I need to find the population of Tokyo.
Action: search("Tokyo population 2024")
Observation: Tokyo has a population of approximately 14 million...
Thought: Now I have the answer.
Action: finish("Tokyo has about 14 million people")

Plan-and-Execute

Generate plan upfront, execute sequentially:

Plan:
1. Search for Tokyo population
2. Search for New York population
3. Compare the two
4. Report findings

Executing step 1...

Multi-Agent

Specialized agents collaborating:

  • Orchestrator: Coordinates tasks
  • Researcher: Gathers information
  • Coder: Writes and executes code
  • Critic: Reviews and improves

Practical Implementation

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Callable
import json

@dataclass
class Tool:
    name: str
    description: str
    function: Callable
    parameters: Dict[str, Any]

class SimpleAgent:
    """ReAct-style agent with tools"""

    def __init__(self, llm_client, tools: List[Tool], max_iterations: int = 10):
        self.llm = llm_client
        self.tools = {tool.name: tool for tool in tools}
        self.max_iterations = max_iterations
        self.memory = []

    def generate_system_prompt(self) -> str:
        tool_descriptions = "\n".join([
            f"- {t.name}: {t.description}"
            for t in self.tools.values()
        ])

        return f"""You are a helpful AI assistant that can use tools to accomplish tasks.

Available tools:
{tool_descriptions}

To use a tool, respond with:
Thought: [your reasoning]
Action: [tool_name]
Action Input: [json input]

When you have the final answer, respond with:
Thought: [your reasoning]
Final Answer: [your answer]

Always think step by step before acting."""

    def parse_response(self, response: str) -> Dict:
        """Parse LLM response into structured action"""
        if "Final Answer:" in response:
            answer = response.split("Final Answer:")[-1].strip()
            return {"type": "finish", "answer": answer}

        if "Action:" in response and "Action Input:" in response:
            action_part = response.split("Action:")[-1]
            action = action_part.split("Action Input:")[0].strip()
            action_input = response.split("Action Input:")[-1].strip()

            try:
                params = json.loads(action_input)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                params = {"input": action_input}

            return {"type": "action", "tool": action, "params": params}

        return {"type": "unknown", "raw": response}

    def execute_tool(self, tool_name: str, params: Dict) -> str:
        """Execute a tool and return observation"""
        if tool_name not in self.tools:
            return f"Error: Unknown tool '{tool_name}'"

        try:
            result = self.tools[tool_name].function(**params)
            return str(result)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error executing {tool_name}: {str(e)}"

    def run(self, task: str) -> str:
        """Execute agent loop until completion"""
        self.memory = []
        self.memory.append({"role": "user", "content": task})

        for iteration in range(self.max_iterations):
            # Generate LLM response
            response = self.llm.generate(
                system=self.generate_system_prompt(),
                messages=self.memory
            )

            self.memory.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response})

            # Parse response
            parsed = self.parse_response(response)

            if parsed["type"] == "finish":
                return parsed["answer"]

            elif parsed["type"] == "action":
                observation = self.execute_tool(
                    parsed["tool"],
                    parsed["params"]
                )
                self.memory.append({
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": f"Observation: {observation}"
                })

            else:
                # Ask for clarification
                self.memory.append({
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": "Please respond with a proper action or final answer."
                })

        return "Agent reached maximum iterations without completing task."


class PlanAndExecuteAgent:
    """Agent that plans before executing"""

    def __init__(self, llm_client, tools: List[Tool]):
        self.llm = llm_client
        self.tools = {tool.name: tool for tool in tools}

    def create_plan(self, task: str) -> List[str]:
        """Generate a plan for the task"""
        prompt = f"""Create a step-by-step plan to accomplish this task:

Task: {task}

Available tools: {list(self.tools.keys())}

Respond with a numbered list of steps. Each step should be actionable.

Plan:"""

        response = self.llm.generate(prompt)

        # Parse numbered list
        lines = response.strip().split('\n')
        steps = [l.split('.', 1)[-1].strip() for l in lines if l.strip()]

        return steps

    def execute_step(self, step: str, context: str) -> str:
        """Execute a single step"""
        prompt = f"""Execute this step using available tools.

Previous context: {context}

Step to execute: {step}

Available tools: {list(self.tools.keys())}

Respond with the tool to use and its result."""

        response = self.llm.generate(prompt)
        return response

    def run(self, task: str) -> str:
        """Plan and execute"""
        # Phase 1: Planning
        plan = self.create_plan(task)
        print(f"Generated plan with {len(plan)} steps")

        # Phase 2: Execution
        context = ""
        for i, step in enumerate(plan):
            print(f"Executing step {i+1}: {step[:50]}...")
            result = self.execute_step(step, context)
            context += f"\nStep {i+1}: {step}\nResult: {result}\n"

        # Phase 3: Summarize
        summary_prompt = f"""Summarize the results of this task:

Task: {task}

Execution log:
{context}

Final answer:"""

        return self.llm.generate(summary_prompt)

Challenges and Solutions

Reliability

Agents can fail, get stuck, or hallucinate actions.

  • Solutions: Guardrails, validation, fallbacks, human-in-the-loop

Context Management

Long tasks exceed context windows.

  • Solutions: Summarization, selective memory, external storage

Tool Selection

Choosing the right tool for each step.

  • Solutions: Better prompting, tool retrieval, learned routing

Safety

Agents can take unintended actions.

  • Solutions: Sandboxing, approval workflows, capability limits

Best Practices

  1. Start simple: Single-agent, few tools. Add complexity gradually.

  2. Structured outputs: JSON mode, function calling for reliable parsing.

  3. Observability: Log every step for debugging.

  4. Graceful degradation: Handle failures, provide fallbacks.

  5. Human oversight: Keep human in the loop for high-stakes actions.

Summary

Agentic AI extends LLMs with autonomous reasoning and action. Key takeaways:

  • Agents combine reasoning, tool use, and iteration
  • ReAct and Plan-and-Execute are common architectures
  • Reliability, safety, and observability are critical

Further Reading:

  • Yao et al., “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models”
  • AutoGPT, LangChain Agents, CrewAI documentation
  • Wu et al., “AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications”
entry.summary: In 2023, an AI agent autonomously completed a software engineering task that would have taken a human hours—writing code, running tests, fixing bugs, and iterating until it worked. This wasn’t science fiction; it was AutoGPT, one of the first agentic AI systems to capture public imagination.

entry.title: Agentic AI Resources: A 2026 Learning Path

link.title: Agentic AI Resources: A 2026 Learning Path

entry.content:
“The best way to predict the future is to invent it. The second best way is to read the papers of those who are inventing it.”

We are in the Agentic primitives phase. The stack is not settled. There is no “React” or “Django” for agents yet—just a Cambrian explosion of libraries.

This post is a living curriculum for engineers who want to specialize in Agentic Engineering in 2026.

Chapter I: Foundational Papers (Must Read)

If you only read 5 papers, read these using a Deep Research Agent:

  1. ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al., 2022)
    • Why: The “Hello World” of agent loops.
  2. Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools (Schick et al., 2023)
    • Why: How to train models to emit API calls naturally.
  3. Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior (Park et al., 2023)
    • Why: The “Stanford Town” paper. Demonstrates memory, reflection, and social dynamics.
  4. Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models (Wang et al., 2023)
    • Why: Shows how agents can write their own code skills to solve Minecraft.
  5. Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (Shinn et al., 2023)
    • Why: Self-correction loops. “Wait, I made a mistake, let me fix it.”

Chapter II: The Engineering Stack

1. Orchestration Frameworks

  • LangChain / LangGraph: The standard library. Flexible but verbose.
  • CrewAI: High-level, role-based. “You are a Researcher, you are a Writer.”
  • AutoGen (Microsoft): Multi-agent conversations. Great for code generation.

2. Memory & State

  • MemGPT: OS-like memory management (Paging context).
  • Pinecone / Weaviate: Vector Databases for Long-term memory.

3. Evaluation

  • AgentBench: Comprehensive benchmark across environments (OS, Database, Knowledge).
  • GAIA: General AI Assistants benchmark. Hard questions that require reasoning + tools.

Chapter III: The Learning Path (2026 Edition)

How do you go from “Prompt Engineer” to “Agentic Engineer”?

  1. Level 1: The Function Caller
    • Learn OpenAI function calling.
    • Build a bot that can query a SQL database.
  2. Level 2: The Loop Builder
    • Implement ReAct from scratch (no frameworks).
    • Understand Thought -> Action -> Observation.
  3. Level 3: The Tool Maker
    • Build custom tools.
    • Handle auth, error handling, and rate limits within tools.
  4. Level 4: The Architect
    • Build a multi-agent system.
    • Solve the “Infinite Loop” problem (Agent gets stuck).
    • Implement “Human in the Loop” for critical decisions.

Chapter IV: Future Trends to Watch

  • On-Device Agents: Apple Intelligence / Android Gemini Nano. Agents running locally on phones.
  • Digital Workers: Agents as employees. “Hire an outbound sales agent.”
  • Interface-less Apps: Why building a GUI when the agent just calls the API?

Summary

The field is moving fast. The frameworks listed here might be dead in 6 months. But the Physics of Intelligence—Memory, Planning, Tool Use—will remain constant.

“Code is how we tell machines what to do. Agents are how we tell machines what we want.”

entry.title: Deep Research Agents: Automating Literature Review and Synthesis

link.title: Deep Research Agents: Automating Literature Review and Synthesis

entry.content:
“An LLM knows what it was trained on. A Research Agent knows what was published 5 minutes ago.”

Standard RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is brittle. It fetches the top-3 snippets and prays the answer is there. Deep Research Agents (like OpenAI’s Deep Research or Perplexity Pro) go further. They act like a human analyst:

  1. They plan a search strategy.
  2. They read multiple sources.
  3. They follow links recursively.
  4. They synthesize a report with citations.

This post explores the architecture of autonomous information gathering.

Related reading: Builds on The Era of AI Agents by applying it to the specific domain of knowledge discovery.

Chapter I: The Breadth vs Depth Trade-off

A research agent must balance:

  • Breadth: How many disparate queries to run? (“competitors to Nike”, “Nike financial reports”, “Nike recent scandals”)
  • Depth: How deep to click? (Search Result -> Landing Page -> PDF Report -> Footnote).

The Recursive Algorithm

Most research agents use a DFS (Depth-First Search) approach with a “satisfaction” stopping condition.

graph TD
    Goal[User Goal: Analyze Competitors] --> Plan[Generate 3 Sub-Questions]
    Plan --> Q1[Q1: Who are they?]
    Plan --> Q2[Q2: Revenue?]
    Plan --> Q3[Q3: Strategy?]

    Q1 --> Search1[Search: 'Nike competitors']
    Search1 --> Read1[Read: Article 1]
    Read1 --> Follow[Follow Link: 'Adidas Annual Report']

    Q2 --> Search2[...]

Chapter II: The Architecture of Synthesis

Reading is easy. Writing is hard. How do you combine 10,000 words of scraped text into a 500-word cohesive summary?

Map-Reduce Summarization:

  1. Map: Summarize each individual document into key facts relevant to the query.
  2. Cluster: Group facts by theme (e.g., “Financials”, “Product”, “Legal”).
  3. Reduce: Write a paragraph for each theme.

This avoids the “Lost in the Middle” phenomenon where LLMs forget the middle of a long context window.

Chapter III: Citation and Verification

The cardinal sin of research is hallucination. Research Agents must enforce Citation Tracking.

Every sentence in the final output must be back-traceable to a Source ID.

  • Bad: “Revenue grew 20%.”
  • Good: “Revenue grew 20% [Source: 10-K Report, Page 45].”

Implementation Tip: Force the model to generate XML tags <cite id="1"> immediately after facts.

Chapter IV: Building a Toy Research Agent

import time

class ResearchAgent:
    def __init__(self, topic):
        self.topic = topic
        self.knowledge_base = []

    def step_1_plan(self):
        print(f"Planning research for: {self.topic}")
        # Mock LLM call to generating queries
        return [f"{self.topic} history", f"{self.topic} recent news"]

    def step_2_execute(self, queries):
        for q in queries:
            print(f"Searching: {q}...")
            # Mock Search API
            results = [{"title": f"Article about {q}", "url": "http://example.com"}]

            for res in results:
                print(f"  Reading: {res['title']}")
                # Mock Scraper
                content = f"Important fact about {q} found in {res['url']}"
                self.knowledge_base.append(content)

    def step_3_synthesize(self):
        print("\nSynthesizing Report...")
        full_context = "\n".join(self.knowledge_base)
        # Mock LLM Summarization
        report = f"## Report on {self.topic}\nBased on {len(self.knowledge_base)} sources:\n"
        for fact in self.knowledge_base:
            report += f"- {fact}\n"
        return report

agent = ResearchAgent("Quantum Computing")
queries = agent.step_1_plan()
agent.step_2_execute(queries)
print(agent.step_3_synthesize())

Chapter V: Use Cases in Advertising

Why does an Ad Tech engineer care? Creative Strategy.

Instead of guessing what ads to write, a Research Agent can:

  1. “Scan all competitor ads for ‘Running Shoes’ in the last month.”
  2. “Identify the top 3 value propositions used (e.g., ‘Comfort’ vs ‘Speed’).”
  3. “Find 1-star reviews on Amazon to identify user pain points.”
  4. “Propose 5 new ad angles based on gaps.”

This turns “Deep Research” into “High-Converting Copy”.

Summary

Deep Research Agents automate the top of the funnel (Strategy). They don’t just find links; they synthesize knowledge. The next generation of CEOs will have a fleet of these agents reading the entire internet every morning.

“Knowledge is power. Synthesis is leverage.”

entry.title: Funnel Tradeoffs in Advertising: Optimizing Awareness, Conversion, and Retention

link.title: Funnel Tradeoffs in Advertising: Optimizing Awareness, Conversion, and Retention

entry.content:
“Performance marketing harvests existing demand. Brand marketing creates future demand. If you only harvest, you will starve.”

A common tragedy in Ad Tech:

  1. CFO joins. Demands $ROAS \ge 4.0$.
  2. Marketing team cuts TV, YouTube, and “Brand Awareness” because they have low ROAS.
  3. They shift budget to “Retargeting” (showing shoes to people who just looked at shoes).
  4. Short term: ROAS skyrockets to $8.0$.
  5. Long term: New user growth flatlines. The brand dies.

This post explores the Upper Funnel vs Lower Funnel problem and how to solve it mathematically.

Related reading: This connects Incrementality Testing with the strategic budgeting discussed in Online Bid Optimization.

Chapter I: The Funnel Physics

The funnel is a flow metrics problem.

  • Upper Funnel (Awareness): Low Probability of Conversion (pCVR), High Volume.
  • Lower Funnel (Conversion): High pCVR, Low Volume.

The Trap: Last-Touch Attribution gives 100% credit to the Lower Funnel (Search/Retargeting). The Upper Funnel (which introduced the user to the brand) gets 0 credit.

Chapter II: The “Performance Performance” vs “Brand Performance”

We need to split metrics.

Stage Metric Measurement
Lower Funnel CPA, ROAS Attribution / Click Cookies
Upper Funnel Lift in Search Volume, Brand Lift Geo-Experiments / Surveys

The Correlation: \(Volume(Search) \propto Spend(Brand, t-30 \text{days})\) There is a lag. Spending on TV today increases Google Search volume next month.

Chapter III: Modeling the Tradeoff

We can model the total system revenue as a coupled differential equation or a multi-stage regression.

\(NewUsers_t = \alpha \cdot BrandSpend_t + \beta \cdot NewUsers_{t-1}\) \(Conversions_t = \gamma \cdot NewUsers_t \cdot PerfSpend_t\)

If $BrandSpend \to 0$, then $NewUsers \to 0$. Eventually $Conversions \to 0$, no matter how high $PerfSpend$ is.

Optimization with MMM

Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM) estimates the $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ parameters without needing user-level tracking.

Chapter IV: Python Simulator

Let’s simulate the creating vs harvesting dynamic.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def simulate_business(weeks=52, brand_budget=1000, perf_budget=1000):
    # Initial State
    awareness_pool = 10000
    revenue = []

    for w in range(weeks):
        # 1. Brand Marketing feeds the Awareness Pool
        # Cost per Reach = $0.10
        new_aware = (brand_budget / 0.10)
        # Decay: 10% of people forget the brand every week
        awareness_pool = awareness_pool * 0.9 + new_aware

        # 2. Performance Marketing harvests the Awareness Pool
        # Conversion Rate depends of Performance Spend
        cvr = min(0.05, perf_budget / 100000)
        conversions = awareness_pool * cvr

        # Revenue ($50 per sale)
        rev = conversions * 50
        revenue.append(rev)

    return revenue

# Scenario A: Balanced
rev_balanced = simulate_business(brand_budget=5000, perf_budget=5000)

# Scenario B: All Performance (Harvest Strategy)
rev_harvest = simulate_business(brand_budget=0, perf_budget=10000)

plt.plot(rev_balanced, label='Balanced')
plt.plot(rev_harvest, label='All Performance')
plt.legend()
plt.title("The Death Spiral of Pure Performance")
plt.ylabel("Revenue")
plt.xlabel("Week")
# Result: 'All Performance' wins for 5 weeks, then crashes as awareness pool drains.

Chapter V: Agentic Optimization

In the Agentic Era, we don’t just set static budgets. An Allocator Agent monitors the “Health of the Funnel”.

  • Signal: “Brand Search Volume is down 10% YoY.”
  • Action: “Shift 20% of budget from Retargeting to Youtube Reach campaigns.”

This is Full-Funnel Automation.

Summary

The job of the CMO (and the algorithm) is to balance Efficiency (ROAS) and Growth (Reach).

  • Too much Efficiency = Shrinking Business.
  • Too much Growth = Bankruptcy.
  • The Sweet Spot = Using MMM to fund the top of the funnel just enough to feed the bottom.

“Don’t eat your seed corn.”

entry.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Grounded LLM Responses

link.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Grounded LLM Responses

entry.content:
In 2023, ChatGPT confidently told a user that the 2024 Olympics were canceled—because its training data cut off in 2021. LLMs are brilliant, but they’re frozen in time, prone to hallucination, and can’t access your private data.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) solves all three problems by grounding LLM responses in retrieved documents. Instead of relying on what the model memorized during training, RAG retrieves current, relevant information and generates answers from that evidence.

This architecture has become the standard for knowledge-intensive applications—from customer support to legal research to internal knowledge bases. Here’s how it works and how to build it.

Introduction and Motivation

LLMs have remarkable capabilities but significant limitations: they hallucinate, their knowledge has a cutoff date, and they can’t access private data. RAG addresses all three by retrieving relevant documents and incorporating them into the generation process.

Instead of relying solely on what the model memorized during training, RAG retrieves current, relevant information and generates responses grounded in that evidence.

RAG Architecture

The diagram below shows the end-to-end RAG pipeline—from the user query, through retrieval and context construction, to grounded generation:

Figure: RAG architecture connecting the query encoder, vector database, document store, and LLM to produce grounded answers.

Basic Pipeline

Query → Retriever → Top-K Documents → Context + Query → LLM → Response
  1. Query processing: Parse user query
  2. Retrieval: Find relevant documents
  3. Context construction: Format retrieved docs
  4. Generation: LLM produces answer using context

Components

Retriever: Dense retrieval (embedding similarity), sparse (BM25), or hybrid.

Document store: Vector database for embeddings, search index for text.

Generator: LLM that incorporates retrieved context.

Chunking: Split documents into retrievable units (paragraphs, sections).

Mathematical Framework

Retrieval

Given query $q$, retrieve documents maximizing: \(d^* = \arg\max_{d \in D} s(q, d)\)

where $s$ is similarity (dot product, cosine, learned).

Generation with Context

\[P(y | q, D) = P(y | q, \text{top-k}(D))\]

The LLM conditions on retrieved documents.

Joint Optimization

End-to-end RAG: \(P(y | q) = \sum_{d \in D} P(y | q, d) \cdot P(d | q)\)

Marginalize over retrieved documents.

Practical Implementation

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np
import faiss
from typing import List, Dict

class SimpleRAG:
    """Basic RAG implementation"""

    def __init__(self,
                 embedding_model='all-MiniLM-L6-v2',
                 chunk_size=500,
                 chunk_overlap=50):
        self.embedder = SentenceTransformer(embedding_model)
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
        self.chunk_overlap = chunk_overlap
        self.index = None
        self.chunks = []
        self.metadata = []

    def chunk_document(self, text: str, source: str = None) -> List[Dict]:
        """Split document into chunks"""
        chunks = []
        words = text.split()

        for i in range(0, len(words), self.chunk_size - self.chunk_overlap):
            chunk_words = words[i:i + self.chunk_size]
            chunk_text = ' '.join(chunk_words)
            chunks.append({
                'text': chunk_text,
                'source': source,
                'start_idx': i
            })

        return chunks

    def add_documents(self, documents: List[Dict]):
        """Add documents to the index

        documents: List of {'text': str, 'source': str}
        """
        for doc in documents:
            doc_chunks = self.chunk_document(doc['text'], doc.get('source'))
            self.chunks.extend([c['text'] for c in doc_chunks])
            self.metadata.extend(doc_chunks)

        # Build FAISS index
        embeddings = self.embedder.encode(self.chunks, show_progress_bar=True)
        embeddings = embeddings / np.linalg.norm(embeddings, axis=1, keepdims=True)

        self.index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(embeddings.shape[1])
        self.index.add(embeddings.astype('float32'))

        return self

    def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int = 5) -> List[Dict]:
        """Retrieve relevant chunks"""
        query_embedding = self.embedder.encode([query])
        query_embedding = query_embedding / np.linalg.norm(query_embedding)

        scores, indices = self.index.search(query_embedding.astype('float32'), k)

        results = []
        for score, idx in zip(scores[0], indices[0]):
            results.append({
                'text': self.chunks[idx],
                'score': float(score),
                'metadata': self.metadata[idx]
            })

        return results

    def format_context(self, retrieved: List[Dict]) -> str:
        """Format retrieved chunks for LLM context"""
        context_parts = []
        for i, r in enumerate(retrieved):
            source = r['metadata'].get('source', 'Unknown')
            context_parts.append(f"[Source {i+1}: {source}]\n{r['text']}")

        return "\n\n".join(context_parts)

    def generate_prompt(self, query: str, context: str) -> str:
        """Create prompt for LLM"""
        return f"""Answer the question based on the provided context. If the context doesn't contain enough information, say so.

Context:
{context}

Question: {query}

Answer:"""


class AdvancedRAG(SimpleRAG):
    """RAG with advanced techniques"""

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.query_expansion = True
        self.reranking = True

    def expand_query(self, query: str) -> List[str]:
        """Generate query variations (in practice, use LLM)"""
        # Simplified: use the query as-is
        # Real implementation would use LLM to generate variations
        return [query]

    def retrieve_with_expansion(self, query: str, k: int = 5) -> List[Dict]:
        """Retrieve with query expansion"""
        queries = self.expand_query(query)

        all_results = []
        seen_chunks = set()

        for q in queries:
            results = self.retrieve(q, k=k)
            for r in results:
                chunk_hash = hash(r['text'])
                if chunk_hash not in seen_chunks:
                    seen_chunks.add(chunk_hash)
                    all_results.append(r)

        # Sort by score and take top k
        all_results.sort(key=lambda x: x['score'], reverse=True)
        return all_results[:k]

    def rerank(self, query: str, retrieved: List[Dict]) -> List[Dict]:
        """Rerank with cross-encoder (simplified)"""
        # In practice, use a cross-encoder model
        # Here we just return as-is
        return retrieved

    def query(self, question: str, k: int = 5) -> Dict:
        """Full RAG pipeline"""
        # Retrieve
        if self.query_expansion:
            retrieved = self.retrieve_with_expansion(question, k=k*2)
        else:
            retrieved = self.retrieve(question, k=k*2)

        # Rerank
        if self.reranking:
            retrieved = self.rerank(question, retrieved)[:k]

        # Format context
        context = self.format_context(retrieved)

        # Generate prompt
        prompt = self.generate_prompt(question, context)

        return {
            'prompt': prompt,
            'retrieved': retrieved,
            'context': context
        }


# Example usage
documents = [
    {
        'text': """Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence that enables
        systems to learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed.
        It focuses on developing algorithms that can access data and use it to learn for
        themselves. The learning process begins with observations or data, such as examples,
        direct experience, or instruction, to look for patterns in data and make better
        decisions in the future.""",
        'source': 'ML Overview'
    },
    {
        'text': """Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks
        with many layers. These deep neural networks are capable of learning hierarchical
        representations of data. Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in computer
        vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition.""",
        'source': 'Deep Learning Intro'
    },
    {
        'text': """Transformers are a type of neural network architecture that uses
        self-attention mechanisms. Introduced in 2017, transformers have become the
        foundation for most modern NLP models including BERT, GPT, and T5. They are
        particularly effective for sequence-to-sequence tasks.""",
        'source': 'Transformers'
    }
]

# Build RAG system
rag = AdvancedRAG()
rag.add_documents(documents)

# Query
result = rag.query("What is deep learning?", k=2)
print("Retrieved context:")
print(result['context'])
print("\nGenerated prompt:")
print(result['prompt'][:500] + "...")

Advanced Techniques

Query Expansion

Generate multiple query variants:

  • Hypothetical document embeddings (HyDE)
  • LLM-generated query reformulations
  • Synonym expansion

Hybrid Retrieval

Combine dense and sparse: \(s_{hybrid} = \alpha \cdot s_{dense} + (1-\alpha) \cdot s_{sparse}\)

Iterative Retrieval

Multi-hop reasoning:

  1. Retrieve for initial query
  2. Generate intermediate reasoning
  3. Retrieve for refined query
  4. Generate final answer

Self-RAG

Model decides when to retrieve and evaluates its own outputs.

Evaluation

Retrieval Quality

  • Recall@K: Are relevant docs retrieved?
  • MRR: Rank of first relevant doc

Generation Quality

  • Faithfulness: Is answer supported by retrieved docs?
  • Relevance: Does answer address the question?
  • Hallucination rate: Unsupported claims

Best Practices

  1. Chunk wisely: Semantic boundaries, not arbitrary splits.

  2. Optimize retrieval first: Generation can’t fix bad retrieval.

  3. Include citations: Help users verify claims.

  4. Handle no-context gracefully: When nothing relevant retrieved.

  5. Monitor and iterate: Track failure modes in production.

Summary

RAG grounds LLM responses in retrieved evidence. Key takeaways:

  • Retrieval quality determines overall quality
  • Chunk documents semantically for better retrieval
  • Hybrid and advanced techniques improve robustness

Further Reading:

  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”
  • Gao et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey”
  • LangChain, LlamaIndex documentation

entry.title: The Era of AI Agents: From Chatbots to Systems That Act

link.title: The Era of AI Agents: From Chatbots to Systems That Act

entry.content:
“The future of AI isn’t just generating text; it’s doing work.”

For the past decade, AI has been a function: $y = f(x)$. Input image, output label. Input text, output translation. But starting 2024, AI became a system. It can plan, use tools, and correct its mistakes. This is the Agentic Era.

This post moves beyond LLMs (Large Language Models) to LAMs (Large Action Models).

Related reading: This is the culmination of systems thinking from Simplifying ML Systems applied to generative AI.

Chapter I: The Definition of an Agent

A Chatbot answers questions. An Agent achieves goals.

Chatbot: “How do I check the weather?” $\to$ “You can check weather.com.” Agent: “Check the weather in NYC and if it’s raining, cancel my dinner reservation.” $\to$ Actually cancels the reservation via API.

The Agentic Loop

The core architecture is the OODA Loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act):

  1. Thought: What do I need to do?
  2. Action: Call a tool (Calculater, API, Bash).
  3. Observation: Read the tool output.
  4. Repeat: Until goal is met.

Chapter II: The ReAct Pattern

Introduced in Yao et al. (2022), ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) is the “Hello World” of agents.

Instead of just acting or just reasoning, the model interleaves them.

Prompt Template:

Question: [User Goal]
Thought: [What should I do first?]
Action: [Tool Name]
Observation: [Tool Output]
...
Final Answer: [Result]

Python Implementation

import openai

def simple_agent(question):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful agent. Available tools: [calculate, search]."}
    ]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": question})

    while True:
        # 1. Thought (Model Decision)
        response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(model="gpt-4", messages=messages)
        text = response.choices[0].message['content']
        print(f"Agent: {text}")
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})

        # 2. Check if done
        if "Final Answer:" in text:
            return text.split("Final Answer:")[1].strip()

        # 3. Action (Mock execution)
        if "Action: calculate" in text:
            expression = text.split("Action: calculate")[1].strip()
            observation = str(eval(expression)) # Risks! Use safe eval in prod
            print(f"Tool Output: {observation}")

            messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Observation: {observation}"})

Chapter III: The Tool layer

Agents are only as good as their hands (tools). Common tools:

  1. Search: Google/Bing API for ground truth.
  2. Code Interpreter: Python sandbox for math/data analysis.
  3. RAG (Retrieval): Access to private documents.

The Interface Protocol: To use tools, the model often needs an explicit schema (like OpenAI Functions or Tool Use API). It outputs JSON: {"tool": "calculator", "args": {"expression": "2+2"}}

Chapter IV: Memory and State

LLMs are stateless. To be agents, they need Memory.

Short-Term Memory

  • The context window (128k tokens).
  • Stores the immediate chain of thought.

Long-Term Memory

  • Vector Stores (Pinecone, Weaviate).
  • “Procedural Memory”: Storing successful plans to reuse later (Reflection).

The MemGPT architecture treats the context window as RAM and VectorDB as Hard Drive, paging information in and out.

Chapter V: Multi-Agent Systems

One agent is good. A team is better. In frameworks like CrewAI or AutoGen, agents specialize:

  • Researcher Agent: Scours the web.
  • Writer Agent: Synthesizes the draft.
  • Critique Agent: Reviews the draft against guidelines.

They communicate via message passing, effectively simulating a human organization.

Summary

We are moving from “Prompt Engineering” to “Flow Engineering”. The value is no longer just the model weights; it’s the State Machine that wraps the model.

“The future of software is not writing code; it’s defining goals.”

entry.title: Ad Tech Metrics Explained: CTR, CVR, ROAS, and Incrementality

link.title: Ad Tech Metrics Explained: CTR, CVR, ROAS, and Incrementality

entry.content:
“In God we trust. All others must bring data.” — W. Edwards Deming “In Ad Tech we trust. All others must understand conversion lag.” — Anonymous

Ad Tech is notorious for its alphabet soup of acronyms. But these aren’t just jargon—they are the physics of the marketplace. Understanding eCPM is as vital to an ad engineer as $F=ma$ is to a physicist.

This post explains the key metrics, how they relate, and the statistical traps that ruin dashboards.

Related reading: These metrics feed the Online Bid Optimization controllers.

Chapter I: The Hierarchy of Metrics

Everything flows from the Auction to the Bank Account.

1. The Auction Currency: eCPM

effective Cost Per Mille (thousand impressions). This is the only thing the ad server cares about. It normalizes all bids (CPC, CPA, CPM) into a single revenue number for the publisher.

\[eCPM = \frac{Revenue}{Impressions} \times 1000\]

If Bidder A pays $1.00 per Click with $1\%$ CTR: \(eCPM = \$1.00 \times 0.01 \times 1000 = \$10.00\)

2. The Efficiency Metrics (Advertiser View)

  • CPC (Cost Per Click): $\frac{Spend}{Clicks}$. Measures “Traffic Cost”.
  • CPA (Cost Per Action): $\frac{Spend}{Conversions}$. Measures “Acquisition Efficiency”.
  • ROAS (Return On Ad Spend): $\frac{Revenue}{Spend}$. Measures “Business Value”.
    • Good for e-commerce (Sales).
    • Target: $4.0x$ (spend $1, make $4).

3. The Supply Metrics (Publisher View)

  • Fill Rate: $\frac{Ads Shown}{Ad Requests}$. “Did we waste the opportunity?”
  • Viewability: % of ads actually seen by user (IAB standard: 50% pixels for 1s).

Chapter II: The Lagged Conversion Trap

Scenario: You launch a campaign on Monday.

  • Monday Spend: $1000.
  • Monday Revenue: $500.
  • Monday ROAS: $0.5x$ (Disaster!)

Tuesday: User who clicked Monday finally buys.

  • Monday Revenue (updated): $2000.
  • Monday ROAS: $2.0x$ (Success!)

Most conversions happen days after the click. This is Conversion Lag. If you optimize based on today’s reported ROAS, you will kill your best campaigns because they haven’t matured yet.

The Solution: Cohort Analysis

Always analyze based on Click Date, not Conversion Date.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_cohort_roas(df):
    """
    df has columns: click_date, conversion_date, spend, revenue
    """
    # 1. Group Spend by Click Date
    daily_spend = df.groupby('click_date')['spend'].sum()

    # 2. Group Revenue by Click Date (Critical!)
    # Even if conversion happened 7 days later, it belongs to the click cohort
    daily_revenue = df.groupby('click_date')['revenue'].sum()

    # 3. Calculate Mature ROAS
    roas = daily_revenue / daily_spend

    return roas

# Simulating Lag
clicks = pd.date_range(start='2025-01-01', periods=10)
spend = np.random.uniform(1000, 2000, 10)
revenue_immediate = spend * 0.5
revenue_delayed = spend * 1.5 # Comes 3 days later

# If we looked at data on Day 1, we'd see 0.5 ROAS.
# If we looked on Day 5, the first cohort would show 2.0 ROAS.

Chapter III: Attribution Windows

When does credit expire?

  • Click-Through Window: 7 days (Standard). If I buy 8 days after clicking, ad gets 0 credit.
  • View-Through Window: 1 day. If I saw the ad (didn’t click) and bought tomorrow.

Trap: “View-Through” is often 90% cannibalization. See Incrementality Testing at Scale for why View-Through ROAS is usually a lie.

Chapter IV: Simpson’s Paradox in Ad Tech

Aggregated data lies.

Device Spend Revenue ROAS
Android $100 $200 2.0
iOS $1000 $1000 1.0
Total $1100 $1200 1.09

If you optimize for “Total ROAS”, you might cut Android budget because it’s small, or cut iOS because it’s inefficient. But maybe Android users are just cheaper to acquire?

Lesson: Always slice metrics by Dimension (OS, Country, Placement) before making decisions.

Summary

Metrics guide the algorithms.

  • eCPM rules the auction.
  • ROAS rules the budget.
  • Lag rules the reality.

“If you torture the data long enough, it will confess.” — Ronald Coase
